Field notes 03 · 9 June 2026

Why the status stays green

Honest at the bottom, green at the top: how bad news loses its words on the way up.

A programme status goes from green to red in a single step. No yellow in between.

The week before, the report said on track. The trouble had been building for weeks, but nothing in the report had shown it.

Green was the most reasonable thing each person in the chain could write.

A programme reports upward through layers, and at each layer someone decides what to pass on. Bad news is the hardest to move up, because moving it means saying the problem is no longer local.

Nothing is falsified. People pass on the part they can defend: the work is still on track. The condition behind it, harder to explain, is shortened, softened, or left behind. They still expect to fix it themselves before anyone steps in.

At the bottom the report is honest and specific: it will be on track if the data we are still waiting for arrives.
One level up: on track, with a dependency.
Two levels up: on track.

By the second summary, the condition is gone. The status is still green.

Name a problem plainly and you invite pushback. You already know the answers: it is not that bad, nobody senior has flagged it, it used to be worse, every programme has hard weeks. So you soften it before anyone else does.

No one decided to hide anything. A yellow status means a conversation, a recovery plan, and sometimes a hit to credibility. A green status avoids all three. The system makes it easier to keep the status green than to make the case for turning it yellow.

So the worry is deferred or worded away, long before it reaches anyone who could move people, time or priorities around. The problem stays at the level least able to solve it.

Leadership reads green as no attention required, but it means no one has yet been forced to name the problem in a way the next layer cannot dilute.

The report stays green until it cannot. Then it turns red, and the cheap options are gone. The time you would have needed to recover was spent keeping the status acceptable.

This is not a reporting discipline problem. Better templates do not fix it. At every boundary, the honest message needs more explanation. The safer version is easier to pass on.

This is the drift: a green status kept alive, one reasonable choice at a time, long after the work stopped matching it. By the time it turns red, the gap between what is green and what is true has been open for weeks.

Anna Chodynicka, DRIFT Partners · First published on LinkedIn, 9 June 2026
